name: ScaleMCP: Dynamic and Auto-Synchronizing Model Context Protocol Tools for LLM Agents
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.06416 [cs.CL], submitted 9 May 2025, 17 pages); also indexed by DBLP as CoRR abs/2505.06416. No peer-reviewed venue identified as of this survey.
authors_affiliation: Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Vamse Kumar Subbiah, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, James A. Burke. Primary (single) affiliation: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), U.S.A. Correspondence: elias.lumer@pwc.com, anmol.b.gulati@pwc.com. The same lead author (Elias Lumer) authored the prior Toolshed / Graph RAG-Tool Fusion work this paper builds on.
code_url: N/A (no official public code repository announced in the paper, on arXiv, or found via web search; the paper releases the algorithm/pseudo-code, system prompts, query-generation prompts, and example tool/synthetic-question tables in the appendix only. The created dataset of 5,000 financial MCP servers is described but no release link is given.)
task_domain: tool-use (MCP tool/server selection, retrieval, and invocation for tool-augmented LLM agents); financial-metric tool-calling is the concrete instantiation. The retrieved MCP servers (tools) are consumed by a downstream LLM agent that plans tool calls and reasons over their outputs.
problem_setting: Online/interactive, single-agent, training-free (plug-and-play, out-of-the-box LLMs and embeddings) tool selection at scale over thousands of MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. The setting targets three stated limitations of prior tool-selection frameworks: (1) they do not integrate MCP servers; (2) they rely on error-prone MANUAL synchronization of a monolithic local tool repository (duplication, inconsistency, inefficiency); and (3) they abstract tool selection BEFORE the LLM is invoked, removing agent autonomy and preventing dynamic re-querying during multi-turn interactions. ScaleMCP instead (a) builds an auto-synchronizing tool storage system that treats live MCP servers as the single source of truth (CRUD-based indexing), and (b) equips the LLM agent itself with an MCP-retrieval tool so it autonomously decides when to search for and add tools to its context/memory and can re-query mid-conversation. Model-provider tool-count limits (e.g., 128 tools) motivate RAG-style tool retrieval. Evaluation is supervised in the sense that user-query instances carry expected (golden) tool calls (3-12 golden tools per query), but the retriever/agent are not fine-tuned.
what_is_retrieved: tools (MCP servers exposed as tools / tool-API documents). Each retrievable item is an MCP tool document comprising tool name, description, and parameter/argument schema, optionally augmented with LLM-generated synthetic questions.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID leaning STATIC-corpus-with-live-sync: the retrievable store is an external corpus of MCP tool documents (5,000 financial MCP servers), NOT an episodic memory of the agent's own experience. However, the store is auto-synchronized to the live MCP servers (single source of truth) via CRUD operations, so the external corpus itself can change as servers are created/updated/deleted. Separately, at inference the agent can 'add tools into its memory' (load retrieved MCP tools into context), a per-session working memory rather than a persistent experiential store.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Completeness-oriented multi-tool recovery layered on top-k retrieval. Queries are predominantly multi-hop and reference multiple golden MCP tools (typically 3-12, sometimes 12 in a single turn), so the objective is to recover the COMPLETE set of needed tools, not just a single best match. The paper explicitly notes a single query embedding cannot capture multiple distinct tool intents (a known multi-hop dense-retrieval failure), motivating agentic query decomposition: the agent calls the MCP Retrieval Tool in parallel (e.g., 5 times, one keyword set per targeted tool) to assemble the full tool set. Retrieval metrics are still reported at fixed K=1/5/10.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over problem-solution cases)
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned within tool selection, tool-applied RAG / Graph-RAG, agentic RAG, and the Model Context Protocol literature.
retrieval_unit: tool-API / MCP tool document. The unit is a single MCP server's tool document = tool name || tool description || tool arguments(parameter schema), optionally with 0/5/10 appended synthetic questions. For TDWA embedding, this document is decomposed into N weighted components (name, description, parameters, synthetic questions).
index_source: Static external corpus that is LIVE-SYNCHRONIZED rather than offline-frozen. The store is built by an auto-synchronization indexing pipeline (Algorithm 1) that reads the current MCP server tool list (single source of truth), computes a SHA-256 hash over name+description+arguments per tool, diffs against existing storage hashes, and applies CRUD: create/index new tools, delete outdated/removed tools, update changed tools. It is offline-induced from tool definitions (no LLMs were used to create the tools themselves; tools generated deterministically from Fortune 1000 companies + yfinance). It is NOT induced from the agent's own test-time trajectories.
index_structure_topology: Storage-system-agnostic; primarily a FLAT vector index in the experiments. The pipeline supports vector database (flat dense vectors, used in all reported experiments), graph database / hybrid Graph-RAG (mentioned for inter-dependent MCP servers, citing the authors' own Graph RAG-Tool Fusion), or a lexical/keyword (BM25) index, chosen by use case. Reported runs use a flat vector store (no graph/hierarchy actually evaluated).
retriever_type: Hybrid / configurable: dense vector search (off-the-shelf embeddings: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large/-3-small/-ada-002, Amazon titan-embed-text-v1, VertexAI text-embedding-005), sparse BM25 lexical search, and hybrid search, all combined with optional reranking. An LLM is used (a) as the agent that issues MCP-retrieval-tool keyword queries (LLM-as-query-issuer / agentic RAG) and (b) as an LLM reranker (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Matching itself is embedding/lexical similarity, not a trained retriever and not generative tool-as-token.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf / training-free). The paper deliberately uses out-of-the-box embeddings and LLMs from OpenAI/Google/Amazon/Anthropic/Meta with no retriever fine-tuning (explicitly contrasting with prior work that fine-tunes retrievers, e.g., ToolLLM, Seal-Tools). The only 'learned' weighting is the manually-set TDWA component weights (var-1=[0.2,0.2,0.2,0.4], var-2=[0.2,0.3,0,0.5]); these are hand-specified, not learned. Future-work mentions LLM fine-tuning for tool discovery but it is not done here.
query_construction: Agent-issued keyword search queries. The LLM agent is equipped with a 'get_mcp_servers' / MCP Retrieval tool and, per the system prompt, decomposes the user request and passes in keyword query strings to search for specific tools, using PARALLEL tool calling (one search call per tool it wants), e.g., 5 keyword sets for 5 targeted financial metrics. On the index side, tool documents are enriched with LLM-generated synthetic questions (document expansion). Retrieval-experiment queries are the standalone user-query instances (often multi-hop / multi-company).
query_granularity: Two-level / both: task-level user query that the agent decomposes into multiple per-tool (sub-)queries issued in parallel; effectively per-targeted-tool query granularity within a single agent turn, and the agent can re-query across turns. Indexing-side keys are also multi-view (multiple synthetic questions per tool).
when_to_retrieve: active / agent-initiated (adaptive). Retrieval is not a fixed pre-LLM pipeline stage; the LLM agent autonomously decides when to call the MCP Retrieval tool, can call it multiple times in parallel, and can RE-QUERY the storage system if no successful matches are found or across multi-turn conversation. (The retrieval-only Experiment 1 and the agent Experiment 2 also include a static one-shot top-k=5 retrieval as a baseline/comparison point.)
retrieval_trigger_signal: agent-initiated request: the LLM, guided by its system prompt ('the only way to use the tool knowledge base is to use get_mcp_servers'), decides to invoke the MCP Retrieval tool, how many parallel searches to issue, and whether to re-query when matches are insufficient during multi-turn interactions. There is no fixed schedule, token-confidence, or learned-classifier trigger; the trigger is the LLM's own function-calling decision.
reranking: Yes, evaluated extensively. Reranking stages compared: Cohere cross-encoder reranker (rerank-v3-english), and LLM rerankers GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.7. Reranking is the single most impactful lever, especially LLM rerankers, which give the strongest retrieval scores (patching low vector-only recall in the multi-hop setting). Hybrid search (vector+BM25 fusion) is also evaluated as a configuration.
retrieved_context_refinement: Primarily rerank (cross-encoder or LLM reranking over the candidate pool) plus index-side document enrichment via synthetic-question augmentation and TDWA component weighting. The agentic loop adds query decomposition (multiple parallel sub-queries) and the ability to re-query. No explicit reason-in-documents distillation or compression of retrieved tool documents is applied.
tool_document_engineering: Synthetic-question augmentation + weighted-field embedding (TDWA). Each tool document is enriched with 0, 5, or 10 LLM-generated synthetic natural-language questions (conditioned on a {company} template filled with company name/ticker/alias). SQ=10 consistently improves retrieval. The novel Tool Document Weighted Average (TDWA) embeds each component (name, description, parameters, synthetic questions) separately and takes an L2-normalized weighted average (weights sum to 1), rather than concatenation or unweighted averaging, to control each component's contribution in vector space.
index_content_separation: Partial / progressive disclosure at invocation time: the lightweight tool index (embedded tool documents) is retrieved first; only the retrieved (top-k=5) MCP servers' full tool definitions are then loaded into the LLM context and 'bound' to the LLM via function calling for actual execution, separating the searchable index from the heavier bound tool set used on demand. Within an index entry there is no further index-vs-content split.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Core contribution: LIVE auto-synchronized tool index with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the integration protocol. MCP servers are the single source of truth; an auto-synchronization pipeline performs CRUD (create, read, update, delete) on the storage index based on SHA-256 hash diffs of tool name+description+arguments, eliminating manual updates to a monolithic local repository. Tools are served via MCP-compliant servers (fast-mcp / FastMCP framework). Retrieved tools are bound and invoked through OpenAI-compatible function calling over the bidirectional MCP connection. This contrasts with prior static RapidAPI/RESTful tool stores.
tool_dependency_awareness: Limited / optional. The default reported setup treats MCP servers as independent (scaled via a vector database). The paper notes that if MCP servers are dependent on each other, a graph database / hybrid Graph-RAG approach (citing the authors' own Graph RAG-Tool Fusion) can encode dependency information for retrieval, but no inter-tool dependency graph is actually constructed or evaluated in this paper's experiments.
how_retrieved_used: prompt/tool-space augmentation via agentic function calling: retrieved MCP servers are loaded into the LLM's context and bound as callable tools; the agent then calls them (in parallel) to obtain tool responses and reasons over those responses to produce the final answer. No fine-tuning; retrieved tools enter the agent's action space and can be re-queried across turns (added to the agent's working tool memory).
planning_integration: Agentic retrieve-act loop / interleaved within the agent invocation: rather than retrieve-then-plan as a fixed pre-LLM stage, the LLM agent autonomously searches (MCP Retrieval tool, parallel calls), receives candidate tools, binds and invokes them, observes responses, and can re-query/search again, forming a retrieval-augmented planning loop over multiple steps. The paper frames this as moving beyond static top-k single-shot retrieval toward iterative agent-driven tool discovery and invocation.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-tool-call within an agent turn (and across multi-turn conversation): the agent issues multiple parallel MCP-search calls (one per targeted tool) and multiple parallel tool invocations within a turn, and may re-search in later turns. It is coarser than per-CoT-step/per-token interleaving; retrieval is woven in at the granularity of (parallel) tool-search and tool-invocation actions.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved case is adapted/revised). The closest analog is the agent re-querying with new keywords when matches are insufficient.
retrieved_item_representation: raw structured tool/API documents (MCP tool name, description, JSON-style parameter/argument schema) injected into the agent's context and bound as function-calling tools; on the index side these are dense vectors (optionally TDWA-weighted) over the tool-document components.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: tool-level descriptive documentation / single tool-API capability description (name + description + parameter schema, optionally with synthetic questions), i.e., a tool-API document rather than a raw trajectory, distilled strategy, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Mainly reranking-based relevance refinement (cross-encoder / LLM rerankers re-score candidates to suppress weak vector matches) plus agentic re-querying (the agent can search again if no successful matches are found). Synthetic-question enrichment and TDWA weighting aim to improve representation quality. There is no retriever-aware adversarial training, no learned relevance evaluator/self-reflection module (the paper proposes Anthropic's 'think' reflective tool as FUTURE work to mitigate low tool-correctness).
memory_type: Configurable external tool store (vector/graph/lexical) treated as a synchronized tool index, plus a transient per-session agent working memory of bound tools. Not an episodic/experiential or skill/workflow/procedural memory of past task outcomes.
write_back: Partial / not experiential. The system writes to the tool STORAGE INDEX, but only to keep it synchronized with live MCP servers (CRUD create/update/delete on tool definitions), not to store the agent's own task experiences/cases/skills. The agent 'adds tools into its memory' (loads retrieved tools into context) within a session, but this is working memory, not persisted experience.
online_growth: Yes for the tool index, in the sense of auto-synchronization: the store automatically grows/shrinks/updates as MCP servers are created, updated, or deleted (single source of truth), via the CRUD pipeline. No for experiential growth: the store does not accumulate the agent's trajectories or learned cases during deployment.
write_back_trigger: tool-definition change driven (single-source-of-truth sync), not experience-driven. A write/update/delete to the storage index occurs when the SHA-256 hash of a live MCP server's tool (name+description+arguments) does not match the stored hash (create or update) or when a stored tool is no longer present among live servers (delete); matching hashes trigger no operation. The agent never writes its own task experiences back; write-back of agent experience = never.
failure_experience_usage: N/A (no storage/retrieval of successful or failed agent trajectories). Failed retrievals lead the agent to re-query with new keywords within the session, but no failure cases are persisted or later retrieved.
memory_evolution_update: Index entries are mutated only to track the source of truth: refine-overwrite on tool change (delete old hash/entry, re-index new definition), delete/prune on tool removal, create on new tool. There is no merging, delta-accumulation of experience, or link-and-evolve of experiential memory; it is a hash-diff-driven refresh of tool definitions.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. Retrieval/selection is not a trained or RL-optimized policy. It is similarity-based top-k (dense/BM25/hybrid) with optional cross-encoder/LLM reranking, while the WHEN/WHAT-to-search decisions are made by an off-the-shelf LLM via function calling (in-context, untrained for this objective). TDWA weights are hand-set, not learned.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent setting with a private (per-session) bound-tool memory. The MCP tool store is a shared external resource but not a shared experiential memory. The paper discusses Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol and multi-agent ecosystems only as future work.
benchmarks: A newly created (self-constructed) dataset of 5,000 real-world financial-metric MCP servers (tools) plus ~140,000 user-query instances (avg 5.0 tool calls per instance; some queries reference 3-12, up to 15-company, golden tools). Tools were built from Fortune 1000 companies x 5 deterministic templates (current_stock_price, stock_price_history, analyst_price_targets, revenue, net_income) using yfinance and the fast-mcp/FastMCP framework. Evaluations: Experiment 1 (vector-DB retrieval), Experiment 2 (end-to-end LLM agent), Experiment 3 (TDWA weighting). No external/public tool benchmark (e.g., ToolBench, API-Bank) is used for the main experiments.
benchmark_family: tool (tool/MCP-server retrieval and end-to-end tool invocation) -- a self-constructed financial-metric MCP benchmark, not a standard public tool benchmark family (cited related families: ToolBench/ToolLLM, API-Bank, Seal-Tools).
baselines: Internal comparisons across configurations rather than competing external systems. Retrieval methods compared: vector-only search, hybrid search, BM25 lexical search, Cohere cross-encoder reranking (rerank-v3-english), and LLM reranking (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.7); five embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large/-3-small/-ada-002, Amazon titan-embed-text-v1, VertexAI text-embedding-005); synthetic-question counts SQ=0/5/10. Storage/embedding strategies: simple Concat (baseline) vs TDWA var-1 [0.2,0.2,0.2,0.4] vs TDWA var-2 [0.2,0.3,0,0.5]. End-to-end: 10 LLM agents (gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-o4-mini, gpt-o3, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B) x three retrieval strategies (BM25 text search, vector search, vector + Cohere reranker).
key_metrics: Retrieval (Experiments 1 & 3): NDCG, Recall, MAP at K=1/5/10. End-to-end agent (Experiment 2, via the DeepEval framework): Tool Correctness (= correct tool calls / total tool calls, incl. valid args and correct output interpretation) and Task Completion Score (alignment score between expected and generated outputs).
headline_result: End-to-end: gpt-o3 with vector search + Cohere reranking achieved the highest Task Completion of 94.4% (but only 36.1% Tool Correctness); gpt-4o-mini was the most balanced at 54.0% Tool Correctness and 86.7% Task Completion (vector + Cohere reranker). Retrieval: best Recall@10 = 0.94 (VertexAI text-embedding-005 + GPT-4o reranking, SQ=10) and best MAP@10 = 0.59 (same embedding + Claude reranking). A key reported finding is the large gap between high Task Completion and low Tool Correctness on complex multi-hop queries.
ablations: (1) Embedding-model and search-config sweep (Exp 1): vector-only retrieval is weak (MAP ~0.50) under multi-hop supervision; reranking, especially LLM reranking (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7), substantially improves results; BM25 is weakest; SQ=10 synthetic questions consistently beats SQ=0/5. (2) TDWA vs Concat (Exp 3, SQ=10, text-embedding-3-large): in plain vector search Concat slightly wins (NDCG 0.634 / Recall 0.912 / MAP 0.499 vs TDWA var-1 0.631/0.886/0.504 and var-2 0.620/0.891/0.485); gaps narrow under reranking and TDWA var-2 sometimes wins reranked MAP@5 (e.g., Cohere TDWA var-1 MAP 0.528 > Concat 0.510); authors attribute Concat's edge to keyword-heavy tickers and synthetic-query/eval-query co-generation bias, arguing TDWA may generalize better on human queries. (3) Agent retrieval-strategy ablation (Exp 2): cross-encoder reranking consistently improved both Tool Correctness and Task Completion over vector-only/BM25; Llama 3.3 70B failed tool calling entirely (0.0% Tool Correctness); Claude models underperformed on Tool Correctness.
evaluation_decoupling: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG/Recall/MAP @K) are reported separately (Experiments 1 and 3) from end-to-end agent metrics (Tool Correctness and Task Completion, Experiment 2), explicitly decoupling retrieval quality from downstream task success. The paper highlights the divergence (high Task Completion can mask low Tool Correctness).
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both. Process-level: retrieval ranking metrics (NDCG/Recall/MAP) and Tool Correctness (whether correct tools were invoked with valid args and outputs interpreted). Outcome-level: Task Completion Score (whether the final response fulfills the user query regardless of tools used). The paper stresses the gap between the two.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively. LLM reranking gives the strongest recall but is noted as computationally expensive (a 'patch' over weak vector recall); future work aims to show agent-driven ScaleMCP retrieval can match/exceed reranked performance at lower inference cost and higher transparency. The dataset design (templating ~100 base queries per tool across companies; deterministic tool generation) is emphasized as cost-efficient and reproducible. Agentic parallel tool-search/invocation is used to scale beyond the 128-tool provider cap. No concrete latency, dollar-cost, or token-count numbers are reported.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed top-k retrieval at k=5 for the agent experiments (retrieved MCP tools passed in via OpenAI function calling). Retrieval metrics reported at K=1/5/10. The agent issues parallel searches (e.g., 5 search calls, one per targeted tool) and can re-query, so the effective number of equipped tools is agent-driven. The motivating constraint is the model-provider limit of <=128 tools per request. No explicit token budget for the bound-tool prompt is given.
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (empirical method/system paper, not a survey).
benchmark_construction_and_size: Self-constructed, LLM-assisted but largely deterministic: 5,000 MCP servers (Fortune 1000 companies x 5 deterministic financial-metric tool templates; tools generated programmatically from structured metadata via yfinance + fast-mcp, NO LLM used for tool creation). Tool documents enriched with 0/5/10 LLM-generated synthetic questions. ~140,000 user-query instances created by writing ~100 base queries per tool and templating across companies (avg 5.0 golden tool calls/instance; complex queries reference 3-12, up to 15 companies). Answers are verifiable against expected tool calls (Tool Correctness) and via alignment scoring (Task Completion via DeepEval). Difficulty signal: even best models hit only 36-54% Tool Correctness despite up to 94.4% Task Completion. No public release link found.
builds_on: Authors' own prior tool-RAG work -- Toolshed: Scale Tool-Equipped Agents with Advanced RAG-Tool Fusion and Tool Knowledge Bases (Lumer et al., 2024/2025a) and Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (Lumer et al., 2025b); Re-Invoke (Chen et al., 2024) for tool-document augmentation; the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024) and FastMCP (jlowin, 2025) as the protocol/serving substrate; agentic RAG (Singh et al., 2025), API-Bank (Li et al., 2023) and AnyTool (Du et al., 2024) for agent-driven dynamic tool discovery; BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) and RAG/Graph-RAG surveys (Gao et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024); off-the-shelf embeddings/LLMs (OpenAI, Google, Amazon Titan, Anthropic, Meta) and function calling (OpenAI, 2024); DeepEval (Confident AI, 2025) for evaluation; Seal-Tools (Wu et al., 2024) for the multi-hop dense-retrieval limitation.
contrasts_with: Static, pre-LLM tool-selection pipelines that abstract retrieval before invocation and remove agent autonomy (incl. the authors' own Toolshed and Re-Invoke as static retrieval pipelines); monolithic local tool repositories requiring manual synchronization (duplication/inconsistency); non-MCP tool frameworks (RapidAPI/RESTful, e.g., ToolLLM/ToolBench, Gorilla); simple embedding concatenation or unweighted averaging of tool-document components (Chen et al., 2024; Lumer et al., 2025a/b) which TDWA replaces with weighted-component embedding; fine-tuned tool retrievers (ToolLLM, Seal-Tools, CRAFT, ToolRerank) which ScaleMCP avoids in favor of out-of-the-box, plug-and-play components.
lineage: Group E (tool-use). A 2025 MCP-native tool-selection/retrieval system in the direct lineage of the authors' Toolshed (RAG-Tool Fusion) and Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, advancing tool retrieval from static, manually-synchronized, pre-LLM pipelines toward (a) a live CRUD auto-synchronized tool store with MCP as the single source of truth and integration protocol, (b) agentic RAG where the LLM autonomously searches/re-queries/binds MCP tools via function calling, and (c) a TDWA weighted-component tool-document embedding refining prior concatenation/averaging tool-document engineering (Re-Invoke, EasyTool). Positioned within the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval sea-change toward dynamic tool stores, MCP/function-calling protocols, and agent-driven tool discovery.
